flashcards.q: What's the precise difference between an image and a container?
flashcards.a: An image is read-only, content-addressed layers plus config metadata. A container is that image plus one writable layer for runtime changes, plus namespaces (pid/net/mnt/uts/ipc/user) and cgroups giving it its own view of the system and resource limits.

flashcards.q: Why does deleting a file inside a running container not shrink the image?
flashcards.a: Image layers are immutable once built. A delete inside a container only writes a whiteout marker in the container's writable layer (or a new layer if committed); the file still physically exists in the earlier read-only layer.

flashcards.q: Why does Dockerfile instruction order affect build speed?
flashcards.a: The build cache invalidates forward from the first changed instruction. Ordering rarely-changing steps (base image, dependency install) before frequently-changing ones (COPY . .) means a code edit only re-runs the final layer instead of reinstalling dependencies.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between a named volume and a bind mount?
flashcards.a: A named volume is Docker-managed storage under /var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data, portable and orchestrator-friendly. A bind mount injects a literal host path into the container -- fast for local dev, not portable to another host.

flashcards.q: Why can't two containers on the default bridge network resolve each other by name, while Compose services can?
flashcards.a: Docker's embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) only works on user-defined bridge networks. Compose always creates one per project; the default bridge created automatically by the daemon does not get embedded DNS.

flashcards.q: What does docker run -m 512m actually configure, mechanically?
flashcards.a: It sets the container's cgroup memory limit (memory.max under cgroup v2). Enforcement is done by the kernel's OOM killer targeting that specific cgroup, independent of overall host memory -- not a Docker userspace check.

flashcards.q: Why does PID 1 inside a container need special signal handling?
flashcards.a: PID 1 in a namespace gets no default signal handlers installed automatically, so an app without an explicit SIGTERM handler ignores it, forcing Docker to wait the full stop grace period (10s default) then SIGKILL. PID 1 must also reap zombie children.

flashcards.q: A shell-wrapped CMD (`sh -c "python app.py"`) ignores SIGTERM and always takes the full grace period to stop. Why?
flashcards.a: The shell becomes PID 1, not the Python process; the signal goes to the shell, which doesn't forward it to its child by default. Fix with exec form (CMD ["python","app.py"]) or `exec` inside the shell script.

flashcards.q: Why does docker system df show different numbers than summing docker images sizes?
flashcards.a: docker images sizes double-count layers shared across images. docker system df reports actual disk usage with shared-layer deduplication and specifically reclaimable space.

flashcards.q: What does exit code 137 mean, and how do you confirm the cause without guessing?
flashcards.a: 137 = 128+9 = SIGKILL was sent to the container's main process, most commonly the OOM killer. Confirm with `docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' <container>` rather than assuming.
